newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - HK, Thai banks in spotlight.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - HK, Thai banks in spotlight.

text.p: Standard Chartered Bank's HK$2.0 billion issue was the big deal in Asian debt markets on Monday, but much attention was focused on troubled Thailand.

Standard Chartered's five-year floating rate certificate of deposit issue was launched at par to float at 30 basis points over the one-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate. With fees, the all-in return is 35 basis points to top-tier participants.
Application will be made to the Hong Kong Monetary Authority to accept the certificates as eligible for its Liquidity Adjustment Facility, or discount window.
Eligibility for LAF makes an issue more attractive to banks because holders of the qualifying debt can engage in repurchase agreements with the monetary authority, increasing liquidity.
The issue also qualifies for a Hong Kong profits tax concession that cuts levies on gains from debt instruments issued in the territory by half to 8.25 percent if they meet certain requirments.
The issue is virtually identical to Standard Chartered Bank's FRCD issued last July. That deal paid 40 basis points all-in for five years.
Pricing for Hong Kong credits has tightened for most Hong Kong credits, but bankers said Hong Kong deals still are viewed as good buys compared with the alternatives.
"As the market does not like Korean or Thai issues, the only deals we can really look at are from the Philippines and Hong Kong," said a syndicate manager at a Japanese bank in Hong Kong.
Korean and Thai issues have lost their lustre as the banking sectors in both countries come under pressure.

Thailand's central bank took action on Monday, announcing that it had ordered commercial banks and finance firms to raise provisions for their sub-standard assets and told 10 finance firms to increase their capital immediately.
The news came on the heels of an announcement that Thailand's largest finance company, Finance One and medium-sized Thai Danu Bank had agreed to merge.

Evelyn Lam, senior credit analyst and head of fixed income research at Banque Indosuez in Hong Kong, said reports of the merger unnerved some investors even though consolidation of the financial sector had been widely anticipated.

"People did not expect that a premium financial company like Finance One would be the first to merge and that sent some shock waves into the investment community about the depth of the problem in the financial industry," she said.

On the positive side, however, the Bank of Thailand's vow to help the financial institutions raise capital was evidence of the government's commitment to maintaining overall systemic stability, said Lam.
She said the merger of Thai Danu and Finance One was positive for both parties, with Thai Danu almost doubling its size and Finance One gaining a foothold in the commercial banking sector.
But some syndicate managers said the merger was not viewed as good news by bankers considering Thai Danu's latest FRCD issue, which was launched last week.
Citing worries about Finance One's exposure to Thailand's troubled property sector, they said the merger could make the the FRCD less attractive.
